title: Not to divide
hook: what he hears here he does not repeat there to set people apart (DN 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mirror, and your line, look in the mirror. Did one breath slip in between a thought and a sentence? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

It starts so innocently. Can I tell you something? Don't say I said this. And then a sentence moves from one room to another, from one friend to the next, and arrives a little bigger than it left. By the end of the week, two people who used to get lunch together aren't speaking, and neither is quite sure why. It can happen in an office, a family, a group chat. The sutta that opens the Long Discourses has a line about exactly this. Today: not to divide.
screen: `DON'T SAY I SAID THIS.` → `ONE ROOM TO THE NEXT.` → `TWO FRIENDS, NOT SPEAKING.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Brahmajala, the all-embracing net, and near its start it lists what an ordinary person might praise in the Buddha. Several of the items are about speech. One is about pisuṇā vācā, divisive speech, the second of the four guards from a few days ago. And the description is precise. What he hears in one place, he doesn't repeat in another to set people there against the people here. What he hears there, he doesn't repeat here. That's the mechanism of gossip, named exactly. Information isn't the problem. Carrying it in order to split people is. The sutta doesn't stop at refusing. It turns the guard into a job. In T. W. Rhys Davids's translation, he lives "as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends". The passage goes on to call him a peacemaker who speaks words that make for peace. So this guard has two halves. Don't carry the sentence that splits. And when you can, carry the sentence that mends. Notice how ordinary this is. No vows, no robes. Just what you do with something you heard by the coffee machine. And notice what it does over time. Over time, people tend to notice who repeats things, and who doesn't. The tradition takes it seriously enough to put it in two places: here on the path, and in the monks' own code, which has a specific offense for tale-bearing between monks.
screen: `PISUṆĀ VĀCĀ: SPEECH THAT SPLITS.` · `HEARD HERE, NOT REPEATED THERE.` · `A BINDER TOGETHER.` · `THE ONE OTHERS TRUST.` · then, large: `NOT TO DIVIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of something you heard recently about someone, the kind of thing that travels. Notice the small pull to pass it on, maybe a little buzz in the chest. Don't fight it. Just feel it, and let it sit there. Then think of the two people it would land between, and picture them still speaking, still getting lunch. Rest in the quiet of a sentence not carried. The bell holds the time.
Not to divide. In the first of the Long Discourses, the Buddha doesn't carry words to split people; he binds together those who are divided.
Your line: not to divide. Today, refuse one piece of gossip, and if you can, carry one sentence that mends. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists treat abstaining from divisive speech as part of right speech; monastics keep a rule against tale-bearing among monks, and some teachers suggest simply letting gossip stop with you.

myth: the sutta's concern is only whether the gossip is true
the concern is purpose: words carried from one side to the other to set people apart.

it calls him a binder together of the divided and a speaker of words that make for peace.

fork.setup: a friend leans in: "don't tell anyone, but Sam said your idea was dumb." what does the Brahmajala picture?
options: pass it on to Sam's other friends.
let it stop with you, and look for a way to mend.
confront Sam in front of everyone.
fork.reveal: DN 1 describes the Buddha as not carrying words from there to here to set people apart, and as a binder together of those who are divided.

original.note: Pali pisuṇā vācā: divisive or slanderous speech, the second of the four kinds right speech gives up.

trapdoor: what you thought: divisive speech means insults.
what it means: carrying what you heard from one side to the other, to split people apart.
what a scholar hears: DN 1 lists it among the 'minor' moral qualities people praise in the Buddha, and Rhys Davids rendered the positive side as 'a binder together of those who are divided'.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1 (Brahmajala Sutta), the section on slander
sources.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, part I
sources.quoted: as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends

notes: Check Rhys Davids's exact wording in Dialogues of the Buddha I (1899), DN 1 §9: 'Thus does he live as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends, a peacemaker, a lover of peace...'. The voice paraphrases the preceding 'what he hears here he repeats not elsewhere...' sentence rather than quoting it.
Pacittiya 3 (bhikkhupesuñña): confirm numbering and that it concerns tale-bearing among monks.
DN 1 frames these as qualities an ordinary person would praise in the Tathāgata (the 'short section on morality').

Editor review: cut the sweeping 'everyone has watched this happen / most of us have carried' and the superlative 'very first sutta' framing; dropped the 1899 date from the spoken line; softened the unsourced claim that the one who doesn't repeat things 'becomes the person others trust'; the practice no longer tells the listener what the pull feels like; howItsDone softened.
